title: Exam format & how the 2025/26 papers look
body:
Course 080931 (Algebra & mathematical logic). What the recent papers in the folder show:

- **Midterm (Nov 2025)** and **prefinal (Dec 2025)**: one theory question — *"state and prove one and only one of the following theorems"* (choose 1 of 2) — plus two exercises.
- **Final (Jan 2026)**: three exercises (FOL resolution: ground + unification; the same claim via tableau; a relations exercise: epi-mono factorization, generated equivalence, induced order) **plus** two theorems to state and prove (soundness of propositional resolution; consistency lemma for FOL resolution).
- The theorems come from the official **"List of theorems with proof"** (List 1 easier / List 2 harder) — see the next section. Chapter 4 (algebra) has **no** theorems on the list; algebra appears only in exercises.
- Instructions on every sheet: *theoretical justification must be provided for each answer in concise but complete form*.

**Exercise patterns that recur almost verbatim:**
1. "Use resolution (ground, then unification) to prove $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$" for a relation property (serial+symmetric+transitive ⇒ reflexive; reflexive+circular ⇒ symmetric; reflexive+op-transitive ⇒ transitive; composition of "surjective" relations).
2. "Same claim with a tableau / semantic tree."
3. "Prove $\Gamma$ satisfiable / $F \not\models \varphi$ by semantical means" → build a small finite structure.
4. Relation on $\{1,\dots,n\}$: reflexive-transitive closure, generated order or induced order, Hasse diagram, epi-mono factorization.
5. Matrix rings: subring, ideal (as a kernel!), quotient ≅ something via the first isomorphism theorem.

Older (2015, instructor L. Mauri) exams also asked to formalize statements and write **SPASS** programs — not seen in 2025/26 papers.

title: Theorem list (state & prove)
body:
From *Theoretical exam program* ("still subject to modifications"). Numbers are the program's; the current lecture notes number some of them slightly differently (e.g. soundness of resolution is Thm 2.178 in the notes).

| Ch. | List 1 (easier) | List 2 (harder) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Existence of the equivalence closure (1.86) | Analytic construction of the equivalence closure (1.87) |
| 1 | Stability of equivalences (1.102) | Induced order (1.127) |
| 1 | First isomorphism theorem (1.156) | Epi factorization lemma (1.149) |
| 2 | Hintikka's lemma (2.111) | Consistency posets are contained in finitary ones (2.114) |
| 2 | Maximal elements are Hintikka (2.112) | Compactness (2.117) |
| 2 | Resolution is sound (2.180) | Consistency poset of a regular inference (2.151) |
| 2 | Resolution defines a finitary inference relation (2.185) | Expansion of variants in resolution (2.183) |
| 3 | Commutativity of quantifiers (3.64) | Evaluation and substitution (3.81) |
| 3 | Equisatisfiability of skolemization (3.94) | Satisfiability lemma (3.86) |
| 3 | Hintikka's lemma (3.101) | Consistency lemma for resolution (3.122) |
| 4 | none | none |

**Already asked:** soundness of resolution (midterm 2025 and Jan 2026), compactness (midterm 2025), Hintikka FOL / evaluation & substitution (prefinal 2025), consistency lemma for resolution (Jan 2026), maximal elements are Hintikka and regularity of resolution (July 2023).

**Proof shapes to memorize:**
- *Soundness*: each rule preserves satisfaction (substitution lemma on generalized clauses) ⇒ closed expansion ⇒ unsatisfiable.
- *Hintikka (prop/FOL)*: define the valuation/Herbrand structure from the atoms in $H$; prove $P = \{\varphi : \varphi \in H \Rightarrow \text{true}\}$ is everything by structural induction for uniform notation.
- *Consistency-poset proofs* (compactness, consistency lemma, regular ⇒ consistency poset): check the 5 (prop) or 7 (FOL) conditions one by one, each by contradiction.

title: Relation calculus with incidence matrices
body:
A relation $R : A \rightharpoonup B$ is a subset of $A \times B$; for finite sets use its **incidence matrix** $M(R)$ (row = source, column = target).

| Operation | Meaning | Matrix |
|---|---|---|
| composition $RS$ (diagrammatic: first $R$ then $S$) | $x\,RS\,z \iff \exists y\,(xRy \land ySz)$ | boolean product $M(R)M(S)$ |
| opposite $R^{\mathrm{op}}$ | swap pairs | transpose $M(R)^T$ |
| $R \cap S$, $R \cup S$ | | entrywise $\wedge$, $\vee$ |
| identity $I$ | diagonal | identity matrix |

Properties: reflexive $I \subseteq R$; symmetric $R^{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq R$; transitive $R^2 \subseteq R$; antisymmetric $R \cap R^{\mathrm{op}} \subseteq I$. A **function** $f$ has exactly one 1 per row: $I \subseteq ff^{\mathrm{op}}$ (total) and $f^{\mathrm{op}}f \subseteq I$ (single-valued). Injective: $ff^{\mathrm{op}} = I$; surjective: $f^{\mathrm{op}}f = I$.

**Kernel pair** of $f$: $K = ff^{\mathrm{op}}$ ($x K y \iff f(x) = f(y)$) — always an equivalence. For a general relation, $RR^{\mathrm{op}}$ relates elements with a **common image** (symmetric, but not necessarily transitive!).

**Images along $f : A \to B$:** direct image $f_*R = f^{\mathrm{op}}Rf$; inverse image $f^*S = fSf^{\mathrm{op}}$ ($x\,f^*S\,y \iff f(x)\,S\,f(y)$). Adjointness: $f_*R \subseteq S \iff R \subseteq f^*S$. Inverse images of equivalences are equivalences ("stability").

title: Equivalences, closures, quotients & epi-mono factorization
body:
- **$P$-closure** of $R$: smallest relation with property $P$ containing $R$ (unique if it exists; exists when $P$ is stable under arbitrary intersections and the total relation has $P$ — this is how the **existence of the equivalence closure** is proved).
- **Analytic construction:** reflexive closure $R \cup I$; transitive closure $\bigcup_{n\ge1}R^n$; reflexive-transitive $R^{rt} = \bigcup_{n\ge0}R^n$; **equivalence closure** $R^e = (R \cup R^{\mathrm{op}})^{rt}$. On a finite set iterate matrix powers until they stabilize.
- Shortcut: the equivalence generated by $R$ has as classes the **connected components** of the (undirected) graph of $R$.
- Quotient $A/E$ with projection $p : A \to A/E$; $\ker p = E$. Equivalences on $A$ ↔ partitions of $A$ ↔ kernel pairs of surjections.

**Epi-mono factorization of $f$** (recipe used in Jan 2026):
1. Compute $M(ff^{\mathrm{op}}) = M(f)M(f)^T$ → classes of $\ker f$.
2. $p : A \to A/\ker f$ the projection (one column per class).
3. $m = p^{\mathrm{op}}f$, i.e. $M(m) = M(p)^T M(f)$ — the injection from classes to $B$.
4. Check $f = pm$; $p$ surjective, $m$ injective. Unique up to isomorphism.

**First isomorphism theorem:** $f$ induces a bijection $A/\ker f \cong f(A)$. Algebraic version: for a morphism of $T$-models, $\ker f$ is a congruence and $M/\ker f \cong \mathrm{im} f$ as $T$-models.

title: Generated order, induced order, Hasse diagrams
body:
**Recipe** for "smallest order containing $R$; if none, the induced order" (midterm 2025, Jan 2026):
1. Draw the graph of $R$; compute $T = R^{rt}$ (reachability incl. self). On paper: row $x$ of $M(T)$ = everything reachable from $x$.
2. Antisymmetry test: $M(T) \wedge M(T)^T \le I$? A cycle in $R$ ($5 \to 7 \to 6 \to 5$) breaks it.
   - If antisymmetric: $T$ **is** the smallest order containing $R$.
   - If not: **no order contains $R$** (any order containing $R$ contains $T$).
3. Induced order: $E = T \cap T^{\mathrm{op}}$ (mutual reachability = strongly connected components) is an equivalence; $p : A \to A/E$; the **induced order** is $p^{\mathrm{op}}Tp$ on $A/E$ — collapse each cycle to one point.
4. **Hasse diagram:** keep only covering pairs (no loops, no edges implied by transitivity). The official solutions put $x$ **below** $y$ when $x\,T\,y$ (Jan 2026: $[3] \to [1]$ is drawn with $[1]$ on top; midterm 2025: $[1]$, which reaches everything, at the bottom). State your orientation explicitly anyway.

Vocabulary: maximal/minimal (nothing strictly above/below), maximum/minimum (comparable to and above/below everything; unique), sup/inf, chains, Zorn's lemma (inductive poset has a maximal element), total order, well order, monotone maps.

title: Uniform notation (α, β, γ, δ)
body:
| Type | Formula | Components |
|---|---|---|
| α (conjunctive) | $\varphi \land \psi$ | $\varphi,\ \psi$ |
| α | $\lnot(\varphi \lor \psi)$ | $\lnot\varphi,\ \lnot\psi$ |
| α | $\lnot(\varphi \to \psi)$ | $\varphi,\ \lnot\psi$ |
| α | $\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$ | $\varphi \to \psi,\ \psi \to \varphi$ |
| β (disjunctive) | $\varphi \lor \psi$ | $\varphi,\ \psi$ |
| β | $\lnot(\varphi \land \psi)$ | $\lnot\varphi,\ \lnot\psi$ |
| β | $\varphi \to \psi$ | $\lnot\varphi,\ \psi$ |
| γ (universal) | $\forall x\varphi$, $\lnot\exists x\varphi$ | $\varphi[t/x]$, $\lnot\varphi[t/x]$ for **any** closed term $t$ |
| δ (existential) | $\exists x\varphi$, $\lnot\forall x\varphi$ | $\varphi[p/x]$, $\lnot\varphi[p/x]$ for a **new** parameter $p$ |

Rules of thumb: apply **δ before γ** (introduce the witnesses first, then instantiate universals on them); a δ-parameter must not already occur on the branch / in the set; γ can be reused as many times as you like. Double negation $\lnot\lnot\varphi \mapsto \varphi$; $\lnot\top \equiv \bot$.

title: Resolution: propositional and ground (Herbrand-style)
body:
**Goal:** $F \vdash \varphi$ ⇔ $F \cup \{\lnot\varphi\}$ has a **closed expansion** (derives the empty clause $\varnothing$).

**Expansion rules on generalized clauses** (sets of formulas read as disjunctions): α-expansion splits into **two clauses** ($\{\dots,\alpha\} \to \{\dots,\alpha_1\}, \{\dots,\alpha_2\}$); β-expansion replaces $\beta$ with $\beta_1,\beta_2$ **in the same clause**; resolution: from $\{\psi\}\cup X$ and $\{\lnot\psi\}\cup Y$ derive $X \cup Y$.

**Exam table format** (copy it): columns *Step | Formula/Clause | Reason* with reasons like "assumption", "3, δ-expansion", "2, γ-expansion ×3", "14, β-expansion ×2", "7, 15, resolution".

**Ground (first-order, no unification) recipe:**
1. List the premises and the **negated goal** as assumptions.
2. δ-expand the negated goal ($\lnot\forall \to$ new parameters $p, q$).
3. δ-expand existentials you need for witnesses (new parameters each time).
4. γ-instantiate universal axioms **exactly** on the parameters your semantic sketch needs (draw the little diagram first — e.g. $p \to q \to p$ for "serial+symmetric+transitive ⇒ reflexive").
5. β-expand the implications into clauses, then resolve unit clauses against them.

Clauses are **sets**, so duplicate literals merge automatically (ground factoring for free).

title: FOL resolution with unification: prenex → Skolem → clauses
body:
**Pipeline** (the exams want the table *Formula | Prenex form | Skolemization | Clausal form*):
1. **Negate the goal** and add it to the premises.
2. **Prenex form**: pull quantifiers out (rename bound variables apart). $\lnot\forall x\varphi \equiv \exists x\lnot\varphi$, $\lnot\exists \equiv \forall\lnot$.
3. **Skolemize**: each $\exists y$ becomes $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of the universals **to its left**; with none to its left, a constant. ($\forall y\exists x.E(fx,y) \mapsto \forall y.E(f(hy),y)$; $\exists z\forall x.\lnot E(gfx,z) \mapsto \forall x.\lnot E(gfx,p)$.) Skolemization preserves **satisfiability**, not equivalence (Thm 3.94).
4. **Clausal form**: drop $\forall$, CNF, one clause per conjunct. Implications $A \land B \to C$ become $\{\lnot A, \lnot B, C\}$.
5. **Resolve with most general unifiers**; rename variables apart in each clause.

**Strategy:** start from the **negated goal** (it's a unit clause with constants) and resolve it with the axiom whose head matches — SLD-style works because these exercises are Horn. Typical 3–5 step refutations, e.g. reflexive+circular ⇒ symmetric:
$\{\lnot Rqp\}$ + $\{\lnot Rxy,\lnot Ryz,Rzx\}$ → $\{\lnot Rpy,\lnot Ryq\}$ → (with $\{Rxx\}$) $\{\lnot Rpq\}$ → (with $\{Rpq\}$) $\varnothing$.

**Robinson unification:** find disagreement pair, bind a variable to a term **not containing it** (occurs check), repeat.

title: Tableaux and semantic trees
body:
**Tableau:** a tree starting with $F \cup \{\lnot\varphi\}$; α adds both components to the branch, β **splits** the branch, γ adds an instance, δ adds an instance with a new parameter. A branch is **closed** when it contains $\psi$ and $\lnot\psi$ (or $\bot$); mark it ×. All branches closed ⇒ $F \vdash \varphi$.
- Put all non-branching steps (α, δ, needed γ) on the trunk first; branch (β) as late as possible.
- In FOL, instantiate γ on exactly the parameters you introduced.

**Semantic tree:** nodes are **sets of formulas**; at each step expand one highlighted formula (same α/β/γ/δ rules, β splits into two nodes). Leaves that contain a complementary pair are unsatisfiable.
- To prove $F \models \varphi$: every leaf of the tree for $F \cup \{\lnot\varphi\}$ is unsatisfiable.
- To prove $F \not\models \varphi$: find an **open, saturated leaf** — it is satisfiable, and its literals **are a countermodel**: domain = constants used, $[\![R]\!]$ = atoms $R(\dots)$ in the leaf (Sept 2023: $M = \{a,b\}$, $[\![R]\!] = \{a\}$, $[\![S]\!] = \{a,b\}$, $[\![T]\!] = \{b\}$).
- δ on an existential **premise** needs a fresh constant too (that's why $b$ appears).

title: Semantic proofs: satisfiable, not valid, entailment
body:
| Asked | What to show |
|---|---|
| $\Gamma$ satisfiable | **one** structure $M$ with $M \models \Gamma$ |
| $\varphi$ not valid | one structure with $M \not\models \varphi$ |
| $F \models \varphi$ | **every** $M \models F$ satisfies $\varphi$ (argue generally) |
| $F \not\models \varphi$ | one $M \models F$ with $M \not\models \varphi$ |

**Building small models for $R$-puzzles:** translate each formula into graph language (serial = every node has an out-edge; $\forall x\exists y Ryx$ = every node has an in-edge; $\exists x\forall y Ryx$ = a node everybody points to; irreflexive = no loops). Then try 2–3 nodes. Classic answers: the 3-cycle $0\to1\to2\to0$ (serial, irreflexive, "triangle" axioms); the path $0-1-2$ (reflexive symmetric, non-adjacent pairs have a common neighbour); a "hub" element related to/from everything.

**Write-up:** give $M$ and $[\![R]\!]$ explicitly, then check **every** formula, naming the witnesses for each $\exists$ and saying why each $\forall$ holds (including vacuous implications). The 2022 exam explicitly demands "explaining all the details carefully".

Substitution lemma: $[\![\varphi[t/x]]\!](a) = [\![\varphi]\!](a[t/x])$. Commutativity: $\forall x\forall y \equiv \forall y\forall x$, $\exists\exists$ likewise, but $\exists x\forall y \models \forall y\exists x$ only one way.

title: Consistency posets, Hintikka sets, compactness, completeness
body:
**Consistency poset** $C$ (prop.): for every $S \in C$ — (1) not both $x, \lnot x$; (2) $\bot,\lnot\top \notin S$; (3) $\lnot\lnot\varphi \in S \Rightarrow S\cup\{\varphi\} \in C$; (4) $\alpha \in S \Rightarrow S\cup\{\alpha_1,\alpha_2\} \in C$; (5) $\beta \in S \Rightarrow S\cup\{\beta_i\} \in C$ for some $i$. FOL adds (6) γ: $S \cup \{\gamma(t)\} \in C$ for every closed $t$; (7) δ: $S \cup \{\delta(p)\} \in C$ for some new parameter $p$.

**Hintikka set** $H$: same conditions with "$\in H$" instead of "$S \cup \{\dots\} \in C$" (closed downward under the components).

**Chain of results:**
1. Hintikka's lemma: Hintikka sets are satisfiable (prop: $a(x) = 1 \iff x \in H$; FOL: Herbrand structure on closed terms, $[\![R]\!]$ = atoms in $H$).
2. Maximal elements of a consistency poset are Hintikka (maximality turns "$S \cup \{\dots\} \in C$" into "$\dots \in S$").
3. Every consistency poset extends to a finitary/subset-closed one, where Zorn gives maximal elements ⇒ every $S \in C$ is satisfiable.
4. Applications: **compactness** ($C$ = sets whose finite subsets are satisfiable); **completeness** of any **regular** inference ($C$ = consistent sets, $F \nvdash \bot$); **consistency lemma for resolution** ($C$ = finite sets with no closed resolution expansion).

**Regular inference:** $\alpha \vdash \alpha_i$; $\beta,\lnot\beta_1,\lnot\beta_2 \vdash \bot$; $\vdash \top$. Resolution is regular (two 4–6 line expansions), hence complete.

**Soundness ≠ completeness:** soundness = $\vdash \Rightarrow \models$ (rules preserve truth); completeness = $\models \Rightarrow \vdash$ (via consistency posets).

title: Algebra exercises: subrings, ideals, quotients, groups, congruences
body:
**Subring check:** contains $0$ and $1$ (= $I$), closed under $-$ and $\cdot$. Write the generic product and read off the form. **Commutative** iff the product formula is symmetric.
Trick: write matrices as polynomials in a nilpotent/special matrix: $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&a\end{pmatrix} = aI + bN$ ($N^2 = 0$, $\cong \mathbf{R}[x]/(x^2)$); $\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\0&a&b\\0&0&a\end{pmatrix} = aI+bN+cN^2$ ($N^3=0$, $\cong \mathbf{R}[x]/(x^3)$); $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\4b&a\end{pmatrix} = aI + bJ$ ($J^2 = 4I$, $\cong \mathbf{R}[x]/(x^2-4)$).

**Ideal — best proof: exhibit it as a kernel.** Find a ring morphism $h$ with $\ker h = \mathfrak{a}$ (e.g. $A \mapsto a$, $A \mapsto d$, or "evaluate $J$ at $2$": $aI+bJ \mapsto a+2b$). Kernels are automatically ideals and the **first isomorphism theorem** gives $R/\mathfrak{a} \cong \mathrm{im}\,h$ — that's how you prove "$R/\mathfrak{a}$ is a field" or "$R/\mathfrak{a} \simeq k$".
Not an ideal of the bigger ring: find one product that leaves $\mathfrak{a}$.
Direct image of an ideal is an ideal **if $h$ is surjective**; the inclusion of a subring is the standard counterexample otherwise.

**Maps between quotients** $k/\mathfrak{b} \to k/\mathfrak{a}$, $[A]_\mathfrak{b} \mapsto [A]_\mathfrak{a}$: well defined iff $\mathfrak{b} \subseteq \mathfrak{a}$; kernel $\mathfrak{a}/\mathfrak{b}$ (third isomorphism theorem).

**Groups:** subgroup = non-empty, closed under product and inverse. **Normal:** closed under conjugation — or, slicker, the preimage of a normal subgroup under a morphism (e.g. $G \to (\mathbf{R}^2,+)$, $A \mapsto (a,b)$). Isomorphism: compare the multiplication laws and match parameters.

**Algebraic theories ($T$-models):** axioms are universally quantified equations; submodels = subsets closed under all operations; a **congruence** is an equivalence compatible with the operations = kernel pair of a $T$-morphism; $M/\!\sim$ inherits a $T$-structure. Restricting a congruence $U$ on $R$ to a submodel $S$: $U \cap S^2 = \ker(ip)$ is a congruence, and $S/V \hookrightarrow R/U$ (Sept 2023).

title: Formalizing statements (and SPASS, older exams)
body:
**Template:** extend the language with symbols for the objects named in the statement (function symbol $h$, constant $g$, $a$…), then write
$$\text{(theory axioms)} \land \text{(definitions/hypotheses)} \to \text{(conclusion)}.$$

- Group axioms: associativity, $x1 = 1x = x$, $xx^{-1} = x^{-1}x = 1$. Lattice axioms: assoc. + comm. of $\wedge,\vee$, absorption. Order in a lattice: $x \le y \iff x\wedge y = x$ (so "totally ordered" = $\forall xy(x\wedge y = x \lor x\wedge y = y)$).
- "Morphism" = preserves **every** operation of the signature; "automorphism" adds injective + surjective; "kernel is a normal subgroup" = $h(1)=1$, closure under $xy^{-1}$, closure under conjugation.
- Keep existential objects (max, min, a witness element) inside the same quantifier scope as the formulas that use them.
- Relation-algebra statements: translate compositions with an explicit middle variable — $x\,RR^{\mathrm{op}}\,y \iff \exists u(Rxu \land Ryu)$.

**Sanity-check the claim before formalizing.** Feb 23 2015: "$x \mapsto a \wedge x$ is a lattice morphism" is **false** for non-distributive lattices ($N_5$, $M_3$) — say so.

**SPASS (DFG syntax):** `begin_problem(Name).` → `list_of_descriptions.` (name, author, status, description) → `list_of_symbols.` `functions[(mul,2),(inv,1),(one,0)]` / `predicates[(R,2)]` → `list_of_formulae(axioms).` … `list_of_formulae(conjectures).` with `formula(forall([x,y],equal(…,…))).`, connectives `and`, `or`, `not`, `implies`, `equiv`, `exists` → `end_problem.` SPASS proves the conjecture by refuting its negation.
